name: io.github.archestack/mcp
title: Archestack
description: Pick open-source AI tools from live rankings: stack per problem, rising projects, fit checks

tools.name: recommend_stack
tools.description: Turn a problem into an open-source stack: for each layer (model serving, vector database, chat UI, agent framework, coding agent, MCP server...) the best-ranked projects on Archestack (archestack.com) that pass the user's hard needs, each with why (review strengths), trade-offs (weaknesses), score, place, stars, license, GPU, arm64, RAM and outside services. Scores and facts are refreshed twice a day from GitHub, so picks include projects newer than your training data. Name the layers you see in `layers` for the sharpest answer; leave it out and the problem's words pick up to 4 categories. Put hard needs (no GPU, arm64, license) in the filters. Use it when the user asks what to build with, which tools to combine, or how to approach a problem with open source; then call how_to_apply on the pick you recommend.

problem.description: What the user wants to build or solve, in their words, e.g. "chat with our PDFs on a laptop, no cloud"

layers.description: The parts of the stack you already see, as category ids, titles or plain words, e.g. ["model serving", "vector database", "chat ui"]. Leave out and Archestack picks the categories the problem matches.

license.description: License family. permissive: MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD and similar. copyleft: GPL, AGPL, LGPL, MPL. custom: anything else, including no license

no_gpu.description: true: only projects that run without a GPU

arm64.description: true: only projects with an arm64 build (Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi, Graviton)

has_demo.description: true: only projects with a live demo

tools.name: trending
tools.description: What is rising in open-source AI right now: the projects on Archestack (archestack.com) that gained the most GitHub stars in the last 7 or 30 days, from GitHub's daily star counts, with stars gained, growth, category, score and tagline, plus the categories gaining most. Filter by list or category. Use it when the user asks what is new, hot, trending or gaining traction, or wants to know where a field is moving before picking a tool; stars gained show attention, not quality, so weigh them with the score.

window.description: week: the last 7 complete days; month: the last 30

category.description: Only this category: id or title

tools.name: explain_category
tools.description: The landscape of one category on Archestack (archestack.com): what it covers, the leaders with their main strength and weakness, how many projects are permissive, copyleft, run without a GPU or have arm64 builds, the best pick for each need (permissive, no GPU, arm64, live demo, most stars), what is rising in it this week, and thin spots (needs no project meets). Use it when the user wants to understand a field before choosing ("what are my options for vector databases"); for the plain ranking use top_in_category, to pick across several layers use recommend_stack.

category.description: Category id or title, e.g. "vector-db" or "Vector databases"

tools.name: how_to_apply
tools.description: Before recommending or setting up one open-source project: check it against the user's limits (no GPU, arm64, RAM, permissive license only, no outside services, Docker) fact by fact, with a verdict; the start command pinned to a release, variable names and ports; known pitfalls (review weaknesses, score penalties, stale releases, security advisories, failed safety checks, copyleft terms); what in its review matches the use case; and up to 3 projects in its category that fit better. From Archestack's (archestack.com) checked facts, not the project's own marketing. Use it after recommend_stack or whenever the user is about to adopt a named project for a specific job; it never installs or runs anything.

project.description: Project id like "best-of-ai/qdrant", a GitHub repo like "qdrant/qdrant", or a name like "Qdrant"

use_case.description: What the user wants to do with it, to match against its strengths and weaknesses

no_gpu.description: true: the machine has no GPU

arm64.description: true: it must run on arm64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton)

ram_gb.description: RAM the machine has, in GB

permissive_only.description: true: only MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD and similar licenses are allowed

no_outside_services.description: true: it must run without outside services (hosted APIs, a separate database)

docker.description: true: it must ship Docker files

tools.name: search_projects
tools.description: Find open-source AI projects across both Archestack lists by words and filters. Words match names, repos, taglines, categories and the products a project replaces; results rank by how many words match, then exact names, then projects whose name or category holds the words, then by score. Put hard needs in the filters, not the words (no_gpu instead of "without a GPU"). Use it when the user describes a need rather than naming a project; for a ranking of one category use top_in_category, for replacements of a named paid product use alternatives_to.

query.description: Words to look for, e.g. "vector database" or "chat ui ollama". Leave out to rank by score.

category.description: Only this category: id or title, e.g. "vector-db" or "Vector databases"

license.description: License family. permissive: MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD and similar. copyleft: GPL, AGPL, LGPL, MPL. custom: anything else, including no license

no_gpu.description: true: only projects that run without a GPU

arm64.description: true: only projects with an arm64 build (Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi, Graviton)

has_demo.description: true: only projects with a live demo

tools.name: get_project
tools.description: Everything Archestack has on one project: score and the parts it is made of, place in its category, GitHub facts (stars, license, last commit and release, language, Docker, arm64, GPU, RAM, external services, port), project health, demo and docs links, and the review (summary, audience, strengths, weaknesses). Use it when the user names one project and wants the full picture; for only what it takes to install it use deploy_facts, for two or more projects use compare.

project.description: Project id like "best-of-ai/qdrant", a GitHub repo like "qdrant/qdrant", or a name like "Qdrant"

tools.name: deploy_facts
tools.description: The facts an agent needs before installing or deploying one project: Docker files, arm64 build, GPU need, minimum RAM, outside services it needs, web port, what its README says it needs, the start command from its own compose file or README pinned to a release (setup: command, source link, variable names with secret flags, ports), docs and demo links, and upkeep (latest release, releases in 12 months, security advisories, its package). null means Archestack does not know. Archestack does not track hosting cost or deploy templates. Use it right before installing or self-hosting a project; for its score and review use get_project.

project.description: Project id like "best-of-ai/qdrant", a GitHub repo like "qdrant/qdrant", or a name like "Qdrant"

tools.name: top_in_category
tools.description: The ranking of one category, best first, with score and tagline. An unknown category returns the list of categories, so calling it with a guess is a cheap way to learn the category ids. Use it for "what is the best X"; to filter by GPU, arm64 or license, or to search across categories, use search_projects.

category.description: Category id or title, e.g. "vector-db" or "Vector databases"

tools.name: compare
tools.description: Put 2 to 4 projects side by side: score and its parts, place, stars, license, last commit, Docker, arm64, GPU, RAM, external services, strengths and weaknesses. Use it when the user is choosing between named projects ("X or Y"); with only one name, find candidates first with top_in_category or alternatives_to.

items.description: Project id like "best-of-ai/qdrant", a GitHub repo like "qdrant/qdrant", or a name like "Qdrant"

tools.name: check_repo
tools.description: Check a GitHub repo before installing it, most useful for an MCP server, skill or plugin: whether Archestack lists it, its license in plain words, upkeep, the safety checks it passed (with the failed ones and their evidence) and up to 3 higher-ranked projects in its category. "Checks passed" means those checks passed, not that the code is safe. A repo Archestack does not list returns listed: false and a link to suggest it. Use it when the user pastes a GitHub link they plan to install or run; for a project they name without a link use get_project.

tools.name: alternatives_to
tools.description: Open-source projects that replace a paid or closed product (e.g. Cursor, ChatGPT, Notion), highest score first. own_claim is true when the project says so in its own README. Use it when the user names a product and asks what can replace it or how to self-host it instead; to weigh the picks against each other, pass them to compare.
